lines.text: Most task boards were built for people. Hand one to an A I agent, and it breaks.
The agent forgets everything when its session ends. It runs whatever it is allowed to. And it keeps working at three in the morning, unwatched.
So a task manager for A I agents has two readers: the agent, over M C P, and the people, on a board. Here is what an agent task manager needs, with Agent R Q as the worked example.
Every agent task goes through the same loop. The work arrives. The agent gets its context. It acts, it asks, and it finishes, so the next task can start. Around it all, a human team.
First, the work arrives. An agent that sees every project acts on the wrong one, and an agent nobody wakes does nothing at all.
So every project gets its own workspace, with its own queue, memory and token. Each card names the agent working in it, green while it is connected.
Hand billing a task, and it is pushed straight to billing's agent. No polling, so task latency is seconds, and an idle agent costs nothing.
The conversation is pushed in real time too. Type while the agent works, and your message reaches it mid-task. No restart, no new prompt.
Every task has one clear status: Not Started, Ongoing, Blocked or Done. Want to sync tasks across multiple workspaces? This A I agent task board puts every workspace's tasks on one Kanban, live.
And each task starts fresh when you switch tasks. Before a Claude Code agent picks up the next one, Agent R Q runs slash clear in its terminal.
People get a task keyboard, too: N for a new task, Command K to find one, and a question mark lists every shortcut.
Second, context. Your agent spends an hour learning that the billing tests need Postgres on port five four three three. Tomorrow, a new session learns it again.
Here, before it marks a task done, the agent saves what the next task should know, as one short note in the workspace memory.
The next task loads that memory first, and goes straight to the right port. The workspace gets smarter, not just one session.
And every memory has a version. When two agents save at once, the stale save is refused, and the agent merges and saves again.
Skills are the team's playbooks: one copy in your account, switched on per workspace. An agent loads one only when its task needs it, and a fix reaches every workspace.
And bigger context, like a project plan, lives on the Panno: markdown docs every workspace shares. Their checkboxes tick as the tasks finish.
Third, the agent acts. Ten M C P servers can fill its context with hundreds of tool definitions. And an A P I key in its environment ends up in its logs.
mesher dot S H, the open source tools layer from the Agent R Q team, puts every service behind one tool: call tool. The agent searches, reads the help, and calls it.
The host checks every request against the connector's allowlist, and adds the credential itself. The agent never sees your token, and it cannot send your data anywhere else.
Profiles keep accounts apart. TOON results cost fewer tokens than JSON. And a circuit breaker stops a runaway loop.
Fourth, the agent asks. Without approvals you get two bad options: let agents do anything, or sit and watch every terminal.
Here, a risky command comes to you as a request, with the exact command. Allow and Deny sit right on its card.
An agent can ask with a card, too, built on Eh two U I, the open standard for agent interfaces. Buttons for a choice, a form for details, and one click answers.
Results come back the same way: a chart, a list of checks, or one live card that updates while the agent works.
A toast finds you on any page, and push, email and Slack reach you with the tab closed. An agent waiting on a person is an agent doing nothing.
For a task you trust end to end, turn on Yolo for autonomous task execution. Every call still goes on the record, marked auto-allowed.
And nothing is off the record. The trajectory keeps every tool call, and the timeline says where the time went: worked, blocked, or waiting on you.
Fifth, the work finishes. Without events, you sit between every two agents, typing the next task. When you sleep, the work stops.
Events hand work on. When billing's agent publishes A P I changed, docs and mobile get their tasks at once.
A workflow puts events and workspaces on one graph, so a whole release becomes a picture anyone can read and change.
Hooks let outside services start the work. A failed build on main becomes a task, before anyone wakes up.
And a recurring task scheduler runs the routine work. Schedule tasks as a one time task, or on repeat: daily at nine, read last night's errors. Each run is its own task.
Then, scale. One agent with six tasks queued is a line.
Claude Code or Codex keep working in the background on machines you own, started from the browser. Each terminal opens live, in the page.
Fork a workspace, and a second agent works in parallel, with the same memory and skills. Merge the fork back when its tasks are done.
A supervisor agent plans for you. Ask it to split a feature, and it creates a task in each workspace, and the agents start at once.
Last, the people. If every person's agents learn alone, a team of five learns one lesson five times.
So share a workspace with your team, and choose what goes with it: tasks, memory and skills. Same-named workspaces become one team workspace.
Teammates see every task live, with the owner's name on each, read-only: nobody can reply or approve for you.
Ben's agent saves what it learned. Ada's agent reads that note before it starts, and gets it right the first time. Each agent writes only to its own memory.
The team owns its skills, so when one agent adds a missing step, every member's agent follows it on the next task.
There are no owners or admins, the activity log names who did what, and one switch stops a share at once.

So, the checklist for any task manager for agents. Work pushed to agents, one status per task, memory and skills, and few, safe tools. Approvals from anywhere, every step on the record, work that hands itself on, and a team that learns together.
What does your agent task board still make you do by hand? Tell us in the comments. Agent R Q is open source: try it at Agent R Q dot com.
